item.title: Brazil’s data-driven plan for climate-resilient healthcare
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02779-7

By integrating climate risk into health planning, Brazil is redesigning healthcare to withstand floods, heatwaves and other climate shocks.
item.dc:title: Brazil’s data-driven plan for climate-resilient healthcare
item.dc:creator: Lisa Palmer

item.title: Time to drop the no-policy business-as-usual baselines
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02787-7

Baseline construction shapes estimates of mitigation cost, ambition and progress, while no-policy counterfactuals could vary with choices about policy, technology and development. Rather than relying on one constructed baseline, assessments and related conclusions should be compared across plausible baselines.
item.dc:title: Time to drop the no-policy business-as-usual baselines
item.dc:creator: Mel George
Anand Patwardhan

item.title: Zero emissions commitment depends on warming level
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02776-w

The global temperature change that happens after emissions cease is expected to be close to zero. Here the authors use model simulations to show that this zero emissions commitment depends on the warming level at which emissions cease and might be positive for higher warming.

item.title: Southeast Asian voices on climate change
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02783-x

Responding to the increasing risks of climate change in Southeast Asia requires research and effective action that considers the unique challenges of the region. In this Viewpoint, researchers and practitioners from the region share their views on the progress made in understanding and responding to climate change.

item.title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02791-x

The long-term response of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets to warming is often studied using ice-only simulations. Here the authors use a coupled ice–atmosphere–ocean model and find that East Antarctica remains stable even under higher warming because changes in atmospheric circulation increase precipitation sensitivity.
item.dc:title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
item.dc:creator: Kyung-Sook Yun
